It was held concurrently with the [[2014 United States Senate election in Minnesota|election]] to Minnesota's [[Classes of United States senators|Class II U.S. Senate seat]], as well as [[2014 United States Senate elections|other elections]] to the United States Senate in other states, [[2014 United States House of Representatives elections|elections]] to the [[United States House of Representatives]], and various [[2014 United States elections#State elections|state]] and [[2014 United States elections#Local elections|local elections]]. Incumbent [[Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party|Democratic–Farmer–Labor]] governor [[Mark Dayton]] ran for re-election to a second term in office.{{cite web |url=http://www.kare11.com/news/news_article.aspx?storyid=946522 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130127060207/http://www.kare11.com/news/news_article.aspx?storyid=946522 |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 27, 2013 |title=Gov. Dayton stops by KARE 11 Sunrise, says he'll run again in 2014 |date=November 15, 2011 |access-date=November 17, 2012 |work=[[KARE (TV)|KARE]]}} Incumbent Democratic lieutenant governor [[Yvonne Prettner Solon]] retired, and Tina Smith was selected as his new running mate.{{cite news |author=Brian Bakst |title=Minn. Lt. Gov. Prettner Solon says no to 2nd term |newspaper=[[San Francisco Chronicle]] |url=http://www.sfgate.com/news/article/Minn-LG-Prettner-Solon-says-no-to-2nd-term-5141482.php |date=January 14, 2014 |access-date=January 14, 2014}} Primary elections were held on August 12, 2014. Dayton and Smith won the Democratic primary and the Republicans nominated [[Hennepin County, Minnesota|Hennepin County]] [[County commission|Commissioner]] [[Jeff Johnson (Minnesota politician)|Jeff Johnson]] and his running mate former state representative [[Bill Kuisle]]. In the general election, Dayton and Smith defeated them and several other minor party candidates with just over 50% of the vote. Dayton's victory broke his own record, set in 2010, as the oldest Minnesota gubernatorial candidate to win an election; he was 67.{{cite web |url=http://editions.lib.umn.edu/smartpolitics/2014/11/13/minnesotans-elect-oldest-gover/ |title=Minnesotans Elect Oldest Governor, US House Delegation in State History |work=Smart Politics |first=Eric |last=Ostermeier |date=November 13, 2014}} It was also the first gubernatorial race since [[1994 Minnesota gubernatorial election|1994]] in which the winner received a majority of the votes cast. The election was the first time since 1994 that a [[Third party (United States)|third party]] did not gain more than 6% of the total vote. ==Background== Incumbent [[Republican Party of Minnesota|Republican]] governor [[Tim Pawlenty]] declined to run for a third term [[2010 Minnesota gubernatorial election|in 2010]], instead [[Tim Pawlenty 2012 presidential campaign|running for the Republican presidential nomination]] in the [[2012 United States presidential election|2012 election]]. State Representative [[Tom Emmer]] easily won the Republican nomination, and former U.S. senator [[Mark Dayton]] won the DFL nomination with a plurality over [[List of Speakers of the Minnesota House of Representatives|State House Speaker]] [[Margaret Anderson Kelliher]]. After a very close race, Dayton defeated Emmer by just 8,770 votes, 0.42% of all votes cast. Dayton's victory was one of just four that Minnesota Democrats have achieved out of 28 gubernatorial elections during a Democratic presidency.{{cite web |url=http://editions.lib.umn.edu/smartpolitics/2013/12/06/can-dayton-catch-lightning-in/ |title=Can Dayton Catch Lightning in a Bottle Twice? |work=Smart Politics |first=Eric |last=Ostermeier |date=December 6, 2013}} Despite this, and despite his narrow margin of victory in 2010, Dayton was not seen as a top Republican target.
